vignette:
Raj is a 58-year-old South Asian man who came to therapy at his wife's urging, though he was not sure what talking could change. He worked as a product manager for a mid-sized tech firm, a job he had held for over a decade, but in the past year he had begun to feel as though he was barely holding it together. The trouble, he explained slowly, traced back to a single night two years ago, when he was detained and tortured by police during a business trip to a country where he had once lived. For twelve hours, he was held in a concrete room, beaten, and subjected to mock executions while officers shouted at him in a language he only half understood. The incomprehensible chatter of their voices, the dizzying spins of vertigo from a blow to the head, and the distant wail of sirens outside the building had all fused into a single, unbearable memory. He had never spoken of it to anyone, not even his wife, because he was certain that nothing good could come of reopening that night. He believed, with a quiet, unshakable conviction, that there was something fundamentally wrong with him-something that had made the officers choose him, something that made him deserve what happened. That belief had hardened into a general mistrust of everyone around him, and he now assumed that people could not be trusted, that their kindness was always a prelude to betrayal.

Because he felt intrinsically flawed and saw no future worth hoping for, Raj had begun to avoid anything that could possibly be stressful. He stopped attending team meetings where disagreements might arise, delegated every difficult decision to a junior colleague, and declined invitations to social gatherings. He also started monitoring his body constantly, scanning for any sign of dizziness or lightheadedness, which he had come to associate with the onset of a panic attack or, worse, a repeat of the night he could not forget. This body monitoring, in turn, reinforced his sense that something was wrong with him, that his own body was a source of danger. When he saw a police car or a person in uniform on the street, he would cross to the other side or duck into a shop until they passed. These avoidance strategies, though they gave him momentary relief, deepened his conviction that he was broken and that no good could ever come his way again.

His constant vigilance made it impossible to relax. Even at home, in his own living room, he sat with his back to the wall, his shoulders tight, his eyes scanning the room. He woke several times each night to check the locks on the doors and windows, certain that someone had entered. And when his wife touched his shoulder unexpectedly, he would flinch violently, his heart hammering, his breath catching. This startle response was so ingrained that he had begun to sleep on the edge of the bed, facing the door, to avoid being caught off guard. His hypervigilance also made him more sensitive to triggers. The sound of sirens from a passing ambulance would send him straight back to that concrete room, and he would feel the dizziness wash over him again. The incomprehensible chatter of strangers in a coffee shop-just two people speaking another language-would make his palms sweat and his vision narrow. He had come to see these triggers as proof that his body was still in danger, which only made him monitor himself more closely.

The cycle tightened over months. The more he avoided, the more he believed he was fundamentally flawed. The more he scanned for threats, the more triggers he found. The more he found triggers, the more he avoided. His wife began to complain that he was distant, that he no longer laughed or planned for the future. At work, his performance reviews slipped, and he was placed on a performance improvement plan. What finally brought him to seek help was a morning when, after a night of broken sleep, he stood in the kitchen and felt a wave of dizziness so strong he had to grip the counter. He was certain he was about to collapse, and for a moment he thought the police had found him again. He told himself he could not go on like this, but even as he said it, he was not sure he believed that anything could change. What frightened him most was the possibility that the therapy would confirm what he already knew: that he was too broken to be fixed.
